To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the ceiling shape and surface structures of concert halls should be designed such that the early sound arriving at the ears of the listeners in the median plane is as dissimilar as possible from that arriving at the ears in other directions.
the optimum shape of the ceiling of a modern, low‐height, concert hall is a paraboloid, and the optimum surface structure of the ceiling is a series of parallel, horizontal ribs.
the best‐sounding concert halls have ceilings that are shaped like a ’’butterfly’’ and are covered with sound‐diffusing material.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following: (1) the effect of binaural dissimilariy on preference of concert halls, (2) the optimum shapes of concert halls, and (3) the optimum ceiling shapes and surface textures for concert halls.
the design of concert halls that are as free of the ’’dead’’ and ’’boxy’’ character as possible, and with the optimum use of the available ceiling surface to achieve this goal.

the following three aspects: (1) the effect on binaural dissimiliarity of the ceiling shape and the ceiling‐wall angle, (2) the effect on the optimum ceiling‐wall angle of the ceiling shape, and (3) optimum ceiling shapes for concert halls.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the optimum shape for a hall is that which provides the greatest possible binaural dissimility, i.e., the greatest possible difference in the sound reaching the two ears, and that this is achieved with the greatest lateral diffusion possible, which in turn is obtained with the greatest possible ceiling height.

a ceiling shape that is as flat and as narrow as possible, with a sharp and steeply sloping edge, and with a smooth and continuous surface, is the most effective for achieving high listener preference of concert hall acpistoca.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the ceiling should have the following properties: (1) it should not have any large, flat areas, and (2) the ceiling should not have any flat surfaces that are parallel to the median plane of the hall.

a high‐quality concert hall should have a low ceiling and should have as much of the ceiling as possible covered by diffusing material, preferably in the form of a large, curved surface that is at least 3 m above the listener’s head and that is at least as large as the listener’s head.
the optimum ceiling shape for a given hall is one that maximizes the dissimilarity between the binaural responses to sound arriving from the median plane and the lateral sides.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the shape of the ceiling is of paramount importance for the subjective response to music.

, in order to maximize listener preference, the ceiling should be shaped so that it is not only high and narrow, but also so that it is highly dissimilar to a listener’s head, as measured by the Binaural Dissimilarity Index, BD.

, to achieve high listener preference, a hall’s ceiling shape must be such that the early sound energy that arrives at the listener’s ears in median plane is as little as possible, and that the hall’s ceiling shape should be such that the ceiling’s surface structure is as little as is practical.
